data.title: Nitrianske Pravno – Vyšehrad, a hillfort on the Žiar ridge
data.excerpt: On the ridge of the Žiar mountains, on the boundary between the Turiec and the Nitra regions, lies the Vyšehrad hillfort at 829 m above sea level. Its four enclosures, 455 ares in all, were occupied from the end of the Bronze Age through the La Tène period and Great Moravia to a medieval castle whose last inhabitants left in the 15th century — and a song and three legends about Vyšehrad survived among the local people into the 20th century.
data.metaTitle: Vyšehrad near Nitrianske Pravno – hillfort on Žiar ridge
data.metaDescription: The Vyšehrad hillfort at 829 m on the Žiar ridge guarded the old route from the upper Nitra region into Turiec, from the Bronze Age to the 15th century.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: The ridge of the Žiar mountains, the boundary between the Turiec and the Nitra regions, elevation 829 m; cadastral area of Nitrianske Pravno, close to the village of Jasenovo

keyFacts.label: Area
keyFacts.value: A total area of 455 ares, divided by ramparts into four separate enclosures

keyFacts.label: First enclosure
keyFacts.value: The highest-lying part, c. 40 m long — a medieval small fort stood here (12th–14th century); probably fortified and inhabited already in the Great Moravian period and in prehistory

keyFacts.label: Second enclosure
keyFacts.value: An almost regular rectangle of 60 × 40 m with an entrance gateway from the north-west; Slavic, medieval and prehistoric occupation

keyFacts.label: Fourth enclosure
keyFacts.value: The lowest-lying (770 m a.s.l.), a separate structure of 23 × 50 m from the 15th century — built in the last period of the hillfort’s existence

keyFacts.label: Strategic importance
keyFacts.value: A position on the divide between Turiec and Nitra beside an ancient trade route (the Salt/Amber Road) — possibly the original tribal centre of the local Slavs

keyFacts.label: Oral tradition
keyFacts.value: A surviving song about Vyšehrad (bound up with the Mongol invasion of 1241–1242) and several legends about the enchanted lady and the Vyšehrad treasure

keyFacts.label: Researchers
keyFacts.value: K. A. Medvecký (first investigation), Š. Janšák (description and survey, 1928), Marta Remiášová (systematic excavation, 1970s)

timeline.title: The earliest occupation
timeline.description: The earliest population lived in the lowest-lying part of the hillfort; attested by bronze pins, a sickle, an arrowhead and Hallstatt pottery.

timeline.title: Prominent La Tène occupation
timeline.description: The hillfort ranks with the La Tène hillforts of the upper Nitra region, which are evidence of the expansion of the Celtic-Dacian population; a fortification of this period was discovered on the southern side of the hillfort (the Púchov culture).

timeline.title: Rebuilt as a Slavic hillfort
timeline.description: The Slavic population rebuilt the original La Tène fortification according to its own needs; the most important finds (spurs, axes, an axe-shaped currency bar) come from the 9th and 10th centuries.

timeline.title: A less prominent phase of occupation
timeline.description: In this period the four enclosures of the hillfort were used less intensively than in the Great Moravian period.

timeline.title: Rebuilt as a medieval castle
timeline.description: The whole area of the hillfort was rebuilt and repaired on the site of the earlier rampart fortification; a great quantity of finds comes from this period, including weapons and riding equipment.

timeline.title: The end of the Diviaky lordship
timeline.description: After the Mongol invasion (1277) Vyšehrad is mentioned only as a former castle; together with the lordship of the Diviaky family at Vyšehrad its glory came to an end.

timeline.title: A refuge of the army of the Bratríci
timeline.description: A part of the persecuted Hussite Bratríci took refuge at Vyšehrad and fortified themselves there for a time; the royal armies gradually destroyed the Bratríci.

timeline.title: The final departure of the last inhabitants
timeline.description: Coins from the second half of the 15th century scattered throughout the whole area prove that the departure of the last inhabitants of Vyšehrad was not voluntary.

timeline.title: Janšák’s description of the hillfort
timeline.description: Štefan Janšák described and surveyed Vyšehrad in detail and compared its ground plan to a human footprint.

timeline.title: Marta Remiášová’s archaeological excavation
timeline.description: A proper archaeological excavation identified medieval as well as Slavic occupation in all four parts of the hillfort.

children.text: The south-western part of the Malá Fatra passes in the south into the forested Žiar mountains. On the ridge of the Žiar mountains, which forms the boundary between the Turiec and the Nitra regions, lies the Vyšehrad hillfort at an elevation of 829 m, one of the important archaeological and natural sites of the upper Nitra region and of Turiec.

blocks.caption: Vyšehrad, marked on the map of the 2nd military survey
blocks.alt: Vyšehrad, marked on the map of the 2nd military survey

children.text: The most convenient and historically most important crossing from the upper Nitra region into Turiec is the one that leads through the middle part of the Žiar mountains near the village of Nedožery and, at a height of about 300 m, through the village of Brezany in an almost easterly direction along the grassy ridge up to the crest of the Žiar mountains, at a height of 689 m. About halfway along the route there was a coaching inn in the past. This route, however, is not the only crossing from the upper Nitra region into Turiec that links up with the so-called Salt or Amber Road. The second crossing led from Nitrianske Pravno through Vyšehradné, below Vyšehrad, to the village of Jasenovo, and the road continued towards Slovenské Pravno, where the main road now runs.

Because of its natural distinctiveness and its historical importance, and because of its exceptionally important geographical and strategic position on the divide between two regions beside an ancient trade route, Vyšehrad has become a protected natural and archaeological monument. It belongs to the cadastral area of Nitrianske Pravno, but the village of Jasenovo lies considerably closer to it.
Description of the hillfort

On the southern and eastern sides the hillfort is bounded by steep rocks, but access from the western side is also comparatively difficult. The total area is 455 ares. The whole area of the hillfort has a massive rampart fortification and is divided by a system of ramparts into four separate parts, in which we can clearly see enclosures.
The first

, highest-lying part of the fortification, about 40 m long, is divided by a low rampart. This part is separated from the second enclosure by a rampart and a deep ditch. In this part of the hillfort a medieval small fort undoubtedly stood in the 12th–14th century, or rather its uppermost part; yet from the logic and the principles of making use of the possibilities of the terrain for the purposes of defence and fortification it is clear that the upper part must have been fortified and inhabited in the preceding periods as well — those of Great Moravia, La Tène and the Hallstatt period/Bronze Age.
The second
, separate part is interesting for its almost regular rectangular shape (60 × 40 m), with an entrance gateway on the NW side. Slavic, medieval and prehistoric occupation was identified in this part.

blocks.caption: A model of the hillfort after M. Remiášová. Photograph: Pavol Remiáš, TASR
blocks.alt: A model of the hillfort after M. Remiášová. Photograph: Pavol Remiáš, TASR

children.text: The third

part of the hillfort has the most broken terrain, which descends in terraces from the southern side towards the north. This enclosure too is separated from the others by a rampart. This part of the hillfort was likewise used by the Slavs in the period of Great Moravia and also after its demise.
The fourth

part of the hillfort lies lowest. Its elevation is around 770 metres. In this part there is also the entrance to the hillfort from the northern side. On the SW side there is a separate structure measuring 23 × 50 m, bounded prominently on the eastern and northern sides by a rampart and a ditch, in the digging of which a low outer rampart also came into being. It is probably also a functionally separate part of the hillfort, built in the last period of Vyšehrad’s existence, which on the basis of the archaeological finds can be assigned to the 15th century. Objects from the end of the Bronze Age, however, were also found here.

blocks.caption: A model of the hillfort after M. Remiášová. Photograph: Pavol Remiáš, TASR
blocks.alt: A model of the hillfort after M. Remiášová. Photograph: Pavol Remiáš, TASR

children.text: The first to investigate the hillfort was K. A. Medvecký, who found there remains of pottery, stove tiles, an iron arrowhead and nails. The description and survey of Vyšehrad was made by Š. Janšák, well known to us, likewise at the end of the 1920s. We know of older records concerning Vyšehrad from T. Lehotský, P. Petic, J. Novák and P. Florek. A smaller excavation was also carried out here by Dr A. Petrovský-Šichman in 1963.
In 1928 Štefan Janšák described the hillfort as follows:

blocks.text: The geographical shape of the surface of Vyšehrad bears a great resemblance to a human footprint pressed into sand: the SE side forms its toes, the NW side its heel. The course of the ramparts has adapted itself to this natural shape, and by them two entirely separate hillforts are in fact formed: the one on the lower platform, lying 49 m lower than the summit of Vyšehrad, and the enclosures II, III, IV, V, which together form the second group. The hillfort is encircled on the NE and SE by double parallel ramparts a b c, 75 m long, broken at a right angle. On the two remaining sides there is a rocky crag, running almost horizontally along its whole length. The height of the ramparts and the depth of the ditch between them is insignificant, barely 50 cm. The hillfort composed of enclosures II to V is encircled on the outer side by circuit ramparts and by transverse ramparts, and is divided into four enclosures. The height relations of these ramparts are more interesting. The circuit rampart has its lowest point at spot height 790 and from there rises on both sides as far as spot height 829. The transverse ramparts likewise have a considerable fall, adapting themselves to the irregularities of the surface. Only the summit ramparts, in the core of the hillfort, lie almost horizontally. The relative height of the circuit ramparts on the inner side is 2 to 2.5 m. The bottom of the ditch lies about 3 m below the crest of the rampart. The ramparts encircling enclosures IV, V are 0.5 to 1 m high. (note by Orgoň: in the 1970s the archaeologists no longer mention a rampart between enclosures IV and V) Towards the outside, to be sure, one cannot speak of a height, since the artificially created slope of the ramparts merges with the adjoining natural flank of the mountain. The length of the ramparts of this second hillfort amounts to: the circuit ramparts 460 m, the transverse ramparts 120 m.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák
blocks.source: Niektoré novoobjavené hradiská slovenské (Some Newly Discovered Slovak Hillforts), 1928

children.text: In her article Dr Marta Remiášová advances a very interesting consideration: that the name Vyšehrad, its exceptionally important geographical and strategic position on the divide between two regions and beside the ancient route to the Vistula region, suggests that it is here that the original tribal centre of the local Slavs is to be sought. Pavel Dvořák, in turn, states in his Stopy dávnej minulosti 4 (Traces of the Distant Past 4), on page 68, that
“the Poznans had their principal seat in the upper Nitra region, perhaps at Vyšehrad”.
Dr Remiášová’s excavation
A proper archaeological excavation at the hillfort was carried out by Marta Remiášová in the 1970s.

In 1970, in the highest-lying part of the hillfort, medieval occupation with a timber fortification destroyed by fire was identified. The youngest phase of occupation is determined by coins of the 15th century. The fire also destroyed an oven, attested by a concentrated quantity of pottery material and stove tiles. A trench cutting through the rampart drew attention to the fact that the rampart, in whose lowest layer La Tène sherds occurred, had been rebuilt in the Middle Ages, which the coin finds also documented. The inner rampart of the upper part of the hillfort had a timber construction, and on the eastern and northern sides, behind the rampart on its outer face, there was a ditch. The digging out of the ditch probably gave rise to the outer rampart, which is not prominent. The finds from this part are predominantly of the 12th to 15th century; a quantity of various iron objects occurred here: horse harness, hinges, keys, chains, gravers, a sabre hilt, rings, wedges, knives and a great number of nails. Of other materials there were bone ornaments, clay spindle whorls and 25 coins.

blocks.caption: Štefan Janšák’s plan of the hillfort from 1928
blocks.alt: Štefan Janšák’s plan of the hillfort from 1928

children.text: In the course of the evaluation excavation
Slavic material was found in the second and partly in the third part of the hillfort
. Pottery material and remains of timber, especially from the gateway and the rampart, were recovered here. The most important material was precisely that
of the 9th and 10th centuries
, represented by
spurs, axes, an axe-shaped currency bar and some iron objects (nails, small knives, parts of horse harness
). The 13th–15th century is represented in this part of the hillfort as well. The excavation succeeded in identifying the
entrance gateway
into the second part of the hillfort, with post holes for the gate posts and part of a road with stone paving.

At the places on the southern side of the hillfort where the ramparts meet and indicate the possibility of an entrance into the Slavic part of the hillfort, a fortification from the period of La Tène occupation by the Púchov culture was identified. At the time when the fortification was being built it was most probably a single rampart running along the southern side of the hillfort, which is comparatively difficult of access. The rampart was broken through and strengthened in the 9th century. Originally the rampart was built of large stones filled in with small stones and earth. Finds of post holes and the remains of beams draw attention to the fact that
the stone wall had a timber construction.

In the lowest-lying part of the hillfort the earliest phase of occupation was identified, which we have documented by finds of bronze pins, a bronze sickle, a bronze barbed arrowhead and remains of Hallstatt pottery.
A summary of the excavations
Several years of archaeological excavation confirm to us unambiguously that life at Vyšehrad pulsated very vigorously.
The origin of the hillfort
can, on the basis of some finds of bronze objects, be placed as far back as
the end of the Bronze Age and the beginning of the Iron Age

. This is confirmed above all by bronze sickles, bronze raw material, pins, rings and remains of pottery. The territory of the upper Nitra region always had a favourable position and favourable climatic conditions, and therefore Vyšehrad too is one of the many sites that were already occupied in the first millennium BC, around 700 BC. The earliest population at Vyšehrad lived
in the lowest-lying part of the hillfort enclosure
. The hillfort was substantially more intensively occupied in the Late Iron Age
(La Tène)

, and the main part of the material consists of pottery in fragments from large storage vessels and from vase-shaped vessels. Of the other materials there are fragments of glass bracelets, brooches, rings, a large iron knife and other small iron objects of everyday use. For this period of occupation the site can be ranked with the other La Tène hillforts of the upper Nitra region, which are evidence of the expansion of the
Celtic-Dacian population.
That
Vyšehrad was an important centre of the Slavic population in the period of Great Moravia
and in part also after its break-up is proved by distinctly datable finds from this period. Attention may be drawn to
the pottery, iron tools, small axes, small knives, bucket mounts, spurs, an axe-shaped currency bar, an iron bowl

and the other objects. The excavation also established that the Slavic population rebuilt the original La Tène hillfort according to its own needs. Features with the remains of hearths and daub and a quantity of agricultural and craft tools were found at the hillfort. Farmers, shepherds, smiths, weavers and other craftsmen lived and worked here. The weapons and the equipment and armament of horsemen are evidence of the existence of a military retinue which protected the population that lived at the hillfort and in the surrounding Slavic hamlets. The four mutually interlinked enclosures of the hillfort were not used to the same extent in the individual periods in which we have identified the presence of a population. Less prominent phases of occupation come from the 10th and 11th centuries.
In the
12th–14th century

Vyšehrad again found its use, and the whole area of the hillfort and its fortification were rebuilt and repaired on the site of the earlier rampart fortification. A great quantity of finds comes from this whole period. There is pottery, iron objects of everyday use, parts of riding equipment, craft tools and products, items of dress and agricultural implements, and to no small extent weapons. All these objects prove the active life of the population at the castle. According to the situation established, we assume that a castle was built here, within whose precinct log buildings stood. Written reports about Vyšehrad are known from as early as the 13th century, when the whole surrounding area — part of Turiec and of the Nitra side — formed a separate administrative unit which was
administered by the Diviaky family

. From the year 1277 there is a report that after the Mongol invasion Vyšehrad was mentioned only as a former castle. Ladislaus IV granted to master Barleus of Diviaky and his brothers Bošany in exchange for estates in Turiec, among them Vyšehrad, which had been taken from them by his predecessor Béla IV (1235–1270) with a promise of compensation. Together with the lordship of the Diviaky family at Vyšehrad, its glory too came to an end in the years 1235 to 1277.
The fifteenth century was politically turbulent.
The Hussite expeditions

also significantly affected life in the upper Nitra region. The bearer of the aftermath of the Hussite movement in Slovakia was, by virtue of its revolutionary and democratic character, the army of the Bratríci (the Brethren). When, because of its anti-feudal character, it became dangerous to the secular as well as to the divine order, in the years 1458–1467 the royal armies gradually destroyed it. In this period a part of the persecuted Bratríci took refuge at Vyšehrad as well, where they fortified themselves for a time. To these turbulent years must be assigned the
archaeological material of the 15th century

, which consists of weapons, various iron objects, chains, wedges, mounts and tools, parts of horse harness, pottery, a signal horn, and above all coins from the second half of the 15th century. In the course of the excavation we established that the departure of the last inhabitants of Vyšehrad was not voluntary, because precisely those coins which document this period for us were scattered throughout the whole area of the hillfort.

children.text: At this point we could end our account of Vyšehrad without misgivings. That, however, would deprive readers of the extraordinarily interesting information published in his article of 1929 by Peter Petic, which concerns the history of Vyšehrad as the author perceived it at the end of the 1920s. First I bring a few quotations from his article which are without doubt worth noticing.

"It is still told among the people in Pravenec (a little village below Vyšehrad on the Nitra side) that “on Mondays the lads of Pravenec went up to Vyšehrad, made themselves hooks and rang the bells”. So there must still have been towers and bells there for a fairly long time. At Lieština below Vyšehrad a great deal of feverfew is still to be found; according to the tradition of the people, the Vyšehrad lordship used to have its gardens there. "

"In the town archive of Nemecké Pravno there is an old map of Vyšehrad from the year 1779, provided with a Latin–Slovak text. On it we find such names as: “Rivulus subterraneus — the sinking Jasenovo stream”, “Nasedlovom”, “Nakrížikách”, “Lještina”, “Horné vráta”, “Navápenici” and so on. The question arises: why are these names already Slovak at that time? Just as the name “Vyšehrad” itself, so these Slovak names testify only to this: that the castle originates from the 9th–11th century and that it was inhabited by Slovaks."
A Slovak župan at Vyšehrad

“The purpose of our Vyšehrad was originally exclusively the defence and the security of the whole territory belonging to it. Here resided the castellan (comes castrensis), that is to say the župan, who was the administrator of the castle and of the villages belonging to it in time of peace, and the commander of the armed force in turbulent times. All the inhabitants of this territory formed the Vyšehrad castle community, and without doubt they themselves, by their own free resolution, created their castle, for the nobility was as yet unknown in these parts.

The castellan of Vyšehrad could hardly have been given orders and directives by the Zvolen chieftain, who was in one person both personal captain and chief župan of Zvolen, and who under the Árpáds was also supreme commander of several counties and of the castles situated in them; for in that case, why would Béla IV in the middle of the 13th century have demanded Vyšehrad from the Diviaky family, if it had long since been in royal power, which he would not have let out of his hands either. Here the traces of the Slavic lords of Vyšehrad are lost, and it is seized by foreign conquerors, and these are the Diviaky family."

children.text: Besides the valuable observations and reflections given above, the author in 1929 also captured for us the image of Vyšehrad in the consciousness of the Slovak people at the beginning of the 20th century, in the form of a song and of legends bound up with this wonderful place.
A song about Vyšehrad, of which even at that time he was able to record only 2 verses, and which in his opinion is still bound up with the time of the Mongol invasion of Slovakia (1241–1242):

blocks.text:
1. Vyšehrad, Vyšehrad,
the bridges of Vyšehrad,
there lie scattered about
the bones of young lads.

2. The little Vyšehrad of Pravenec is turning green,
rosemary grows upon it, no one picks it,
I shall go and pick it
when it is about to wither.

children.text: Legends about Vyšehrad
1. Legend (Of the enchanted lady of Vyšehrad):

"At Vyšehrad there lived a lady. And since she was beautiful, she had not one but two suitors and lovers. One of them, out of love for her, dug a deep well up there, lined it with fired brick and waited beside it for the white lady to come and draw water. She, however, came neither by day nor by night. After long waiting the jealous man lost his patience and in anger laid a curse upon the whole of Vyšehrad, which immediately sank into the ground; but the lady too remained under the spell.

The people of Pravenec used to go into the forest for mistletoe, wood and raspberries. The men, coming back from the forest, would say: “We have seen the white maiden.” The maiden was dressed in white in the manner of the gentry, a bunch of keys jingled at her belt, her long black hair hung loose down over her shoulders, and on her head she wore a little white hat. When snow was falling she stood beneath a fir tree, and when it stopped falling she walked upon it, leaving behind her the prints of little white slippers.

Once, when the people of Pravenec were thus going for mistletoe, they saw that same white maiden sitting on a “klomec” of mistletoe. An inhabitant of Pravenec, “old Hrnčiar”, called out to her: “Anička, what are you doing there?” He thought it was his beautiful daughter, but Anička gave no answer at all. At the twelfth hour, when the bells are rung, the white lady comes out and runs about the forest with her keys. Whomever she meets, she offers them to him. And she says: “Strike me three times with the back of your hand with these keys.” People, however, do not want to do it, for they think that by this the lady would be freed from the spell, unlocked, and that whoever she gave them to would remain under the spell and would have to walk with those keys for ever. The people of Pravenec frighten their children with this, so that they will be afraid to go into the forest.

On one occasion she showed herself also to shepherds and to raspberry-pickers. Seeing an old man before her, she called to him: “Grandfather, come here, I will give you something”, and added: “Here you shall have whatever you wish.” The old man, however, seeing the bunch of keys with her, answered as follows: “Ah, I am not going there, young lady, you are, I fancy, under a spell there, and if I went there I would set you free and I would damn myself there.” The lady urged the trembling old man: “So you are not coming?” — “I am not coming”, answered the old man. Thereupon a little door opened at the back of the cave, the lady ran inside and no one ever saw her again, for at that moment her bridegroom came, who in an instant freed her from the spell and set her free."
2. Legend (Of the enchanted lady of Vyšehrad):

"Another legend says in turn that the lady of Vyšehrad walks about the forests continually, clad in beautiful black garments reaching down to the ground. From beneath these garments her hen’s claws can be seen. With her goes a great black dog, dragging keys in its jaws, from which it slobbers, so that it seems to be the devil incarnate. Once this lady caught hold of a man and led him to a great tree which from the ground up to its crown had no bark, nor was there any foliage upon it. She showed him this tree with the words: “In this tree, from the bottom up to the top, there is nothing but gold. This gold shall be yours when you strike me three times with the back of your hand with those keys. And should this gold be too little for you, I shall give you also of that which is in the rock.” The man took fright and, sensing devils close by, ran away. That is why the black lady walks about the forests even today, searching and waiting for someone to set her free. "
3. Legend (Of the poor married couple and the treasure of Vyšehrad):

"It happened that in one little village there lived a poor married couple. They suffered great want, and therefore they longed for a better life. Then they heard of the treasures of Vyšehrad, which were now, in the seventh year, due to open. On Good Friday the husband set out for the rock. At that time the rock was to open for the treasures. He waited, but waited in vain, for the rock did not open. Disappointed, he made his way home, but, reckoning on a luckier time, he set out on Christmas Eve. When he got there, the rock was open, and in it lay impenetrable heaps of gold and silver. He leapt inside and took and took into his sacks as much as ever he could, and did not even know which heap he should take from. He ran after the treasures right to the end of the cave; thereupon the rock closed and the good fellow remained inside. There the enchanted people then rocked him in an iron cradle for seven whole years, until the rock opened again. His wife did not know where her husband had gone. She sensed, however, that he was shut up in the rock, and so she waited patiently for seven years and then took up sacks and ran to the rock of Vyšehrad. And indeed, within an hour the rock opened. She leapt inside and at once gathered the treasures into a sack from the very edge and immediately carried them out. She gathered two sacks of money for herself, and at last she snatched her poor husband too out of the iron cradle, by then quite overgrown with moss, and leapt out with him. She rejoiced, for she had both the gold and her husband."
